pages.page_context:
# Knife Shapes and Their Uses Knife shape connects the cook directly to the work. Steel, heat treatment and construction affect how the edge behaves; the blade outline affects how the hand approaches food. Length sets the useful stroke. Height creates knuckle clearance. Curvature favours some movements over others. Thickness affects cutting resistance and how much abuse the blade can tolerate. The point may be a precision tool, a safe rounded end or almost absent. This chapter is **not an exhaustive catalogue of every knife shape**. It covers the forms most common in the Xinzuo range and everyday kitchen work, plus a few useful specialist profiles. Many other regional, historical and specialist shapes exist, but including all of them would make the chapter harder to use. For sales staff, one principle matters more than memorising names: **start from the customer's work, not from the silhouette they like**. Ask what foods they cut most often, in what quantities, whether they work mainly on a board or in the hand, and whether they need broad chopping, long slicing, work around bone, fish preparation or fine detail. These answers identify the blade family that best suits the job. **After choosing the right shape, move to ergonomics.** Ask the customer to hold the knife as they actually cook and compare handle shape, grip position, total weight and balance. Some people prefer a stable, blade-forward knife that feels more forceful in a push cut; others prefer a lighter or more neutral knife that is easy to lift and redirect. The recommendation is complete only when the functional shape is matched to the handle and balance that suit the customer's hand and movement. The breadth of the Xinzuo range makes this comparison practical. Staff can put several technically suitable knives in the customer's hand and compare handle geometry, weight and balance directly. This makes it possible to find a close ergonomic fit instead of treating one handle or balance as universal. Use a clear order: **function first, ergonomics second, specific model third**. Examine the actual blade from heel to tip and consider what its geometry encourages the hand to do. Category names are only guides. Two knives sold under the same name can differ greatly in curve, thickness, balance, bevel geometry and intended motion. No steel grade, finish or specification can make the wrong shape right for the job. A flatter heel and middle give broad board contact and favour push cutting and nearly vertical chopping. A continuous belly lets the contact point travel along the edge during drawing or rocking. A long, narrow blade keeps more edge in contact during a draw slice and reduces drag from the blade face. A narrow point reaches joints and fine details; a broad, supported heel tolerates controlled force better. These are tendencies, not rigid rules: a gyuto can have enough curve to rock, a Western chef's knife can be fairly flat, and a rectangular Chinese-style knife may be a thin general-purpose cutter rather than a bone tool. With these relationships in mind, the main knife families are easier to understand. ## General-purpose knives ### Western chef's knife
The Western chef's knife is a versatile general-purpose form with a continuous belly curve. The curve makes sweeping, drawing and rocking natural, especially when resistance changes through a cut in meat, connective tissue or mixed ingredients. As the knife moves, the working point travels along the belly, combining forward motion with penetration instead of relying only on vertical pressure. It also handles vegetables and fruit well, which is why it became a familiar all-round kitchen tool. Its broad, often substantial blade is usually harder to redirect than a thin narrow slicer once deeply engaged in food. It is a fine cutting tool, not a bone chopper: hard bone, frozen food, twisting and levering are outside its intended use. ### Gyuto
The gyuto overlaps strongly with the Western chef's knife but often has a flatter heel and middle, a slimmer point and less continuous belly. It tends to feel more linear in push cuts and long draw slices and can be easier to steer through small directional changes. Less curvature usually means less progressive rocking than a strongly bellied Western chef's knife, while the slimmer front improves precision. This does not make the gyuto unsuitable for meat or the Western chef's knife unsuitable for vegetables. The difference is one of emphasis. Actual examples vary, so curve, height, thickness and balance matter more than the label. ### Santoku
The santoku is a compact, **primarily vegetable-oriented but highly versatile** knife. Its tall blade, relatively straight heel and middle and lowered front give broad board contact for push cutting and nearly vertical chopping, while enough curve remains for controlled slicing. The height provides knuckle clearance and a useful guiding surface, making it especially comfortable for vegetables, fruit and herbs while still handling boneless meat and fish well. A santoku usually keeps more steel around the front than a fine pointed chef's knife or bunka. This fuller nose gives up some point precision for stronger support and a more stable, blade-forward feel. The hand naturally prepares a firmer stroke when controlling the extra front mass, and the moving blade carries more momentum through resistance. **All else equal, this gives the santoku a more forceful feel in practical push cutting and short vertical chopping.** Its main limitation is compactness: a short edge needs more strokes across a large roast, melon or other wide ingredient, and a very flat santoku is not designed for exaggerated rocking. ### Bunka
The bunka shares the santoku's compact height and board-friendly versatility but ends in an angular **K-tip**. The important feature is not simply a pointed nose: the K-tip places a fine working point low and close to the cutting line, where it is easy to see and control. This combines **the working surface and knuckle clearance of a relatively large blade with front-end precision close to that of a utility knife**. The tip can score skin, enter a small seam, trim delicate areas, make shallow incisions and perform fine directional corrections without sacrificing the broad blade needed for normal board work. The form is especially well suited to **vegetables and fish**, including fine vegetable preparation, trimming, portioning and detail work. It also handles many boneless-meat tasks. The fine K-tip tolerates twisting, levering and hard impact less well than the fuller nose of a santoku; that is the price of added precision. ## Vegetable and Chinese all-purpose knives ### Nakiri
The nakiri is a thin, tall, double-bevel vegetable knife built for broad board contact. Its relatively straight edge makes push cutting and vertical chopping efficient, while its height gives room for the guiding hand and for transferring prepared vegetables. Nakiri fronts vary. Some have a square or only slightly rounded front, while some designs use a deliberately pronounced round tip. On a **round-tip nakiri**, the rounded front is a functional part of the cutting geometry: it is designed to create a stable pivot point for compact rocking movements. The rounded front can remain in controlled contact with the board while the heel rises and falls through a short arc. This gives the knife a compact pivot without requiring the deep belly of a Western chef's knife. The tall blade preserves knuckle clearance and a broad guide for the supporting hand, while the relatively straight working edge behind the pivot returns cleanly to the board. The design therefore combines two useful behaviours in one vegetable knife: **the straight section supports efficient push cutting and chopping, while the rounded front supports controlled compact rocking**. This is particularly effective for herbs, fine vegetable mincing and repeated short board work. Use the round tip as a short, controlled pivot rather than forcing the knife into the wide rocking stroke of a strongly curved chef's knife. Not every nakiri uses this geometry, so examine the actual front profile rather than assuming the same movement from the category name alone. The nakiri is still a thin vegetable cutter and is not intended for bone, frozen food or impact. ### Chinese cleaver
The Chinese cleaver is one of the most distinctive all-purpose forms. Its tall rectangular blade can slice, chop, guide against the knuckles, crush aromatics and transfer prepared ingredients. Examples vary greatly in weight and thickness, so the silhouette alone never proves that a knife can cut bone. Its height, forward mass and lack of a familiar pointed profile can make it harder for beginners because they change the usual visual and tactile references for fine control. In experienced hands, the same features make it exceptionally versatile. Always check weight, thickness behind the edge, bevel geometry and intended use. On the board, a thin all-purpose Chinese cleaver works best with controlled push cuts, short vertical chops and draw slicing rather than heavy impact. The tall face gives excellent knuckle guidance and becomes a convenient scoop for moving prepared ingredients, but the broad blade also magnifies twisting forces if the edge becomes trapped in dense food. Treat a fine slicer as a slicer; use a true bone chopper only when its mass and edge geometry are designed for impact. ### Bone chopper
A bone chopper uses mass, a supported edge and substantial cross-section for controlled butchery where durability and momentum matter more than low-drag slicing. Steels and heat treatments for this work usually favour toughness over extreme hardness because the blade must absorb impact without failing suddenly. It is not indestructible. Large dense bones, hard frozen material, unstable work or a glancing strike can damage the knife and injure the user. A thin Chinese cleaver may look similar while having completely different capabilities. Technique should let the blade's mass do most of the work. Use a stable board, place the target securely and make a committed controlled stroke rather than repeated glancing blows. The thick supported edge is deliberately less delicate than a slicing edge, so using a bone chopper for fine vegetables or thin presentation slices trades accuracy and low drag for strength the task does not need. ## Long carving and slicing knives ### Classic carving knife
A carving knife is longer and narrower than a chef's knife so it can cross a roast, poultry breast, boneless meat or large fruit with fewer strokes. Less blade height reduces drag and improves visibility. The intended movement is a long draw, not repeated short sawing. A useful carving stroke begins with as much of the edge as practical available in front of the food and pulls smoothly through the portion, using blade length instead of downward force. Compared with a chef's knife, the lower blade height gives less knuckle clearance on a board but offers better visibility around a roast and less side contact with the slice. Choose this form when long, clean portions matter more than chopping versatility. ### Roast carving knife
The roast-carving profile keeps a long slicing edge but gives the front a pronounced upward curve. The curve follows the same geometric principle as the belly of a chef's knife: during a mainly horizontal draw, the changing angle of the curved edge creates a progressive downward component at the point of contact. This helps the edge penetrate the meat fibres as the blade moves across them instead of relying only on downward pressure. The curve also follows the rounded surface of a roast and lets the slice finish smoothly as the contact point moves toward the front. It remains a slicer for cooked, boneless food, not a joint breaker. ### Ham knife
A ham knife extends the carving-knife concept. Its very long, narrow blade produces broad thin slices with little friction. Some examples flex slightly to follow the ham; others are firmer. The design excels at long slicing but is inefficient for chopping and small board work. The extra length is valuable only when the cook uses it: start the cut near one end of the edge and let a long, light stroke travel through the meat. Mild flexibility can help the blade follow a broad curved surface, but it is not permission to bend or twist the knife sideways. Compared with a classic carving knife, the ham knife sacrifices some stiffness and general board control for exceptionally long, low-drag slicing. ### Sashimi knife
Long traditional sashimi slicers use their length to cut raw fish in one pulling stroke, leaving a cleaner surface than repeated back-and-forth motion. Traditional examples are single bevelled, normally handed and sharpened differently from ordinary double-bevel slicers. This specialised geometry can steer if the user does not understand the bevel. The technique is intentionally quiet: set the heel, draw the blade toward yourself in one continuous stroke and avoid sawing unless the cut genuinely requires a second pass. The long rigid profile and single-bevel geometry are optimized for surface quality and controlled separation, not for chopping or flexible filleting. Because the reverse face and main bevel form one sharpening system, this knife also demands more specialized maintenance than an ordinary double-bevel slicer. ### Sakimaru
The sakimaru belongs to the same long single-bevel slicing family but ends in a rounded, sword-influenced front. This changes balance, presentation and front access without changing the main task: clean draw slicing through boneless fish. The rounded front is less needle-like than the point of many yanagiba-style slicers, so it is not chosen for piercing small joints or tight detail work. Its value is in how the front completes the long slicing profile and how smoothly the blade can finish a draw through delicate fish. In practical use, blade length, single-bevel geometry and sharpening quality matter more than the ornamental association with a sword-like tip. ### Kiritsuke
In the specialist form shown here, kiritsuke means a long, angular-tipped single-bevel knife for precise slicing and advanced preparation. The K-tip enters delicate cuts accurately. The knife can also be controlled with the index finger extended along the spine toward the front, placing tactile guidance close to the point for shallow incisions and fine directional changes. Do not confuse this traditional single-bevel form with a modern double-bevel kiritsuke-gyuto or K-tip gyuto. The silhouette is not enough; bevel construction and handedness must be stated. ## Boning, filleting and fish butchery ### Western boning knife
A Western boning knife is narrow because boning is a constantly changing three-dimensional cut. The edge must enter beside bone, follow joints, turn around curves, lift connective tissue and repeatedly change angle. A broad blade resists these changes once it is engaged in food. **The very small blade height is fundamental because it lets the blade change angle easily.** The narrow profile also improves visibility and control while tracing joints, removing connective tissue and separating meat from bone. Stiffer versions give deliberate control around beef and pork; more flexible versions follow rounded surfaces more easily. Its main limitation is versatility. The narrow blade gives little knuckle clearance, little food-transfer area and less efficiency in broad board work than a chef's knife, gyuto or Chinese cleaver. Recommend it when boning is a recurring task, not as a general-purpose substitute. Boning means working **around** bone, not chopping through it; twisting the point or using it as a lever can still damage the knife. ### Honesuki
The honesuki is a stiff triangular boning knife used especially for poultry. Its pointed front locates joints and follows bone, while the stronger heel separates connective tissue with controlled pressure. Its compact length and defined point can also help with selected fish-filleting work, especially the first entry beside bone or under membrane. It does not replace a long flexible fillet knife when the task requires bending around a rib cage. Its strengths are almost the opposite: short reach, rigidity and a highly controllable point. ### Fillet knife
A Western fillet knife is long, narrow and often flexible. Its thin cross-section lets the blade follow a rib cage, stay close to skin and move around fish contours while leaving less flesh behind. It is a butchery tool that follows the fish's anatomy before presentation cuts, unlike a long rigid sashimi slicer designed mainly for a clean final draw cut. Flexible models normally use a forgiving balance of toughness and hardness. **A fillet knife made from particularly hard steel needs more caution.** A hard thin blade can flex elastically, but it should never be forced into a deep bend, twisted against hard bone or used to test its flexibility. Excessive lateral stress can cause chipping, cracking or sudden fracture. A break can send the hand and broken edge in an uncontrolled direction, creating a real injury risk. Use only the flex the model is designed to provide. If the knife feels forced rather than naturally following the contour, change the cutting angle instead of bending harder. ### Deba
The deba is a thick, heavy fish-butchery knife. Its strong heel can work through appropriate fish joints and bones with controlled technique, while the front handles finer separation. Traditional deba are single bevelled and handed. Their weight does not make them universal cleavers: large mammal bone, twisting or careless impact can still chip the edge. The deba works by using different parts of the same blade for different operations. The thick heel provides support for controlled work through suitable fish joints and small fish bones, while the thinner front can trace around the head, collar and fillet line with much greater precision. Trying to make the tip perform the heel's impact work, or using the heel like a general-purpose meat cleaver, defeats that division of labour. ## Small, table and precision knives ### Utility knife
The utility knife is between a paring knife and a chef's knife in size and use. It has enough reach for fruit, sandwiches, small vegetables, cheese and boneless meat while remaining agile when a full-size blade would crowd the board. Its narrow profile reduces drag but gives less knuckle clearance and food-transfer area than a chef's knife. It is especially useful in kitchens where many jobs are too large for a paring knife but do not justify the height and reach of a chef's knife: trimming a small roast, portioning citrus, cutting sandwiches or working on a crowded board. The compromise cuts both ways. It is more agile than a chef's knife but less efficient for large volumes, and more capable on a board than a paring knife but usually less comfortable for prolonged in-hand peeling. ### Curved paring knife
The curved paring knife is short enough to control mainly with the fingers. Its pronounced curve follows rounded fruit and vegetables during peeling, coring, blemish removal and decorative shaping. It is especially effective when the ingredient is held safely and the edge must follow a curved surface. The same curve gives less straight board contact. Do not treat it as a miniature chef's knife or force it through pits, joints or frozen food. ### Straight paring knife
The straight paring knife places more of its short edge on the board and tracks a direct cut naturally. It works well on garlic, shallots, small fruit, garnish and exact trimming while remaining compact enough for controlled in-hand work. It follows rounded produce less naturally than a curved parer but is more versatile when preparation alternates between hand and board. In the Xinzuo B30R-SG example shown here, the compact straight profile makes the point easy to place and the short edge easy to control without requiring a large wrist movement. That makes the form useful when precision matters more than stroke length. Its low blade height, however, provides little knuckle clearance, so repeated chopping on a board is better left to a taller knife. ### Steak knife
A steak knife cuts cooked meat at the table, and the choice between a **serrated** and a **plain** edge changes the eating experience. A serrated steak knife can remain **apparently sharp for a long time**. The serration points continue to grip the meat even after repeated plate contact, and the teeth can cut and tear fibres after a smooth edge would feel dull. This makes the knife forgiving in everyday service. The trade-off is a rougher cut: serrations partly tear the meat, disturb its texture and can rupture more cells at the surface, allowing more juice to escape. This may be acceptable for inexpensive or casual service but is less suitable for high-quality meat. For premium steak, a **very sharp plain-edge steak knife** gives a cleaner cut and preserves texture and appearance better. Its weakness is the plate. When every stroke ends against ceramic, the fine apex repeatedly strikes a much harder surface and can lose sharpness quickly. For valuable meat, the best arrangement is simple: **use a sharp plain-edge steak knife and complete the cut on a wooden plate or small food-safe wooden board rather than directly on ceramic**. If ceramic tableware is unavoidable, the edge will need more frequent maintenance. ### Cheese knife
Cheese knives are a family, not one universal shape. Soft sticky cheese benefits from less contact area; a narrow point can portion and serve; hard aged cheese needs stronger support. Openings, hollows and other relief can reduce sticking but cannot eliminate it for every cheese. Choose according to the cheese's texture and size, not the category name alone. Think first about the mechanical problem: soft cheese tends to adhere to broad faces, crumbly cheese rewards a controlled wedge, and very hard cheese needs enough spine and edge support to resist twisting. A cheese knife is therefore best treated as a texture-specific tool rather than a decorative serving pattern. When the cheese is large or dense, stabilize it before cutting; forcing a thin point sideways can damage both knife and food. ## Serrated and hard-food specialists ### Bread knife
Bread-knife serrations solve a simple problem: entering a resistant surface and cutting a soft interior **without compressing it first**. Historically, breadmaking, storage and common loaf styles made this especially useful, but the principle still applies today. The teeth grip the surface so the user can make a light drawing or sawing motion instead of pressing hard downward. Several small contact points let the blade advance with less crushing of the crumb or other soft structure. A pronounced saw profile is **not always necessary** for modern bread. Crust, crumb and freshness vary, and a very sharp plain edge can cut many loaves cleanly. Serrations are most useful when the surface resists first contact but the interior deforms easily. They also work extremely well on brioche, panettone, soft rolls and cake, where downward pressure can deform the product before a plain edge starts the cut. Use a light guided sawing motion and let the teeth work. Excessive pressure crushes the crumb. Serrations often stay functional for a long time because their recesses receive less direct board contact, but sharpening is less straightforward and may require a tapered sharpener or specialist service. ### Frozen-food knife
A frozen-food knife uses strong coarse serrations to saw through suitable frozen ingredients. It exists because forcing a thin hard chef's knife into a frozen block can chip or break the blade. This is still a hazardous specialist operation: stabilize the food, keep the free hand outside the cutting path and avoid twisting or impact. Use the full serrated length with short, controlled strokes and keep the blade aligned with the cut. Do not pry the kerf open or twist the knife when it binds; reposition the food and restart. The specialist geometry reduces the temptation to strike a frozen block with a fine chef's knife, but it does not make every frozen item safe or practical to cut by hand. ## Choosing by work rather than by name For most kitchens, the first serious knife should be a chef's knife, gyuto, santoku or Chinese cleaver whose length and movement feel natural. A bread knife and a small utility or paring knife then cover jobs the main blade handles poorly. Long carving, filleting, fish-butchery and impact tools become worthwhile when those tasks occur often enough to justify dedicated geometry. For sales staff, return to the same questions: **What foods will the customer cut most often? In what quantities? On a board or in the hand? Does the work need broad contact, a long draw, controlled flexibility, a precise point, constant angle changes around bone, or supported mass for impact?** Once the work is clear, the right family of shapes is usually clear too. Then compare ergonomic fit in the customer's normal grip. The next chapter explains why handle grip, intermediate grip and pinch grip can make the same knife feel different, and why Xinzuo offers different balance strategies rather than one universal setup. Choose the profile first and ergonomic fit second. Steel, heat treatment, construction, handle material, appearance and price then complete the choice among models that already suit both task and user. The photographs in this chapter show real Xinzuo versions of the forms discussed. They establish the visible profile, not every property of the knife. Hardness, grind, handedness, heat treatment, balance and bone capability must still be checked on the exact model and understood through the principles in the following chapters.

The height provides knuckle clearance and a useful guiding surface, making it especially comfortable for vegetables, fruit and herbs while still handling boneless meat and fish well.
units.masked_source: The santoku is a compact, **primarily vegetable-oriented but highly versatile** knife. Its tall blade, relatively straight heel and middle and lowered front give broad board contact for push cutting and nearly vertical chopping, while enough curve remains for controlled slicing. The height provides knuckle clearance and a useful guiding surface, making it especially comfortable for vegetables, fruit and herbs while still handling boneless meat and fish well.

units.source: A santoku usually keeps more steel around the front than a fine pointed chef's knife or bunka. This fuller nose gives up some point precision for stronger support and a more stable, blade-forward feel. The hand naturally prepares a firmer stroke when controlling the extra front mass, and the moving blade carries more momentum through resistance. **All else equal, this gives the santoku a more forceful feel in practical push cutting and short vertical chopping.**

units.source: Its main limitation is compactness: a short edge needs more strokes across a large roast, melon or other wide ingredient, and a very flat santoku is not designed for exaggerated rocking.

units.source: The bunka shares the santoku's compact height and board-friendly versatility but ends in an angular **K-tip**. The important feature is not simply a pointed nose: the K-tip places a fine working point low and close to the cutting line, where it is easy to see and control.

units.source: This combines **the working surface and knuckle clearance of a relatively large blade with front-end precision close to that of a utility knife**. The tip can score skin, enter a small seam, trim delicate areas, make shallow incisions and perform fine directional corrections without sacrificing the broad blade needed for normal board work.

units.source: The form is especially well suited to **vegetables and fish**, including fine vegetable preparation, trimming, portioning and detail work. It also handles many boneless-meat tasks. units.source: The nakiri is a thin, tall, double-bevel vegetable knife built for broad board contact. Its relatively straight edge makes push cutting and vertical chopping efficient, while its height gives room for the guiding hand and for transferring prepared vegetables.
units.masked_source: The nakiri is a thin, tall, double-bevel vegetable knife built for broad board contact. Its relatively straight edge makes push cutting and vertical chopping efficient, while its height gives room for the guiding hand and for transferring prepared vegetables.

units.source: Nakiri fronts vary. Some have a square or only slightly rounded front, while some designs use a deliberately pronounced round tip. On a **round-tip nakiri**, the rounded front is a functional part of the cutting geometry: it is designed to create a stable pivot point for compact rocking movements.

units.source: The rounded front can remain in controlled contact with the board while the heel rises and falls through a short arc. This gives the knife a compact pivot without requiring the deep belly of a Western chef's knife. The tall blade preserves knuckle clearance and a broad guide for the supporting hand, while the relatively straight working edge behind the pivot returns cleanly to the board.

units.source: The design therefore combines two useful behaviours in one vegetable knife: **the straight section supports efficient push cutting and chopping, while the rounded front supports controlled compact rocking**. This is particularly effective for herbs, fine vegetable mincing and repeated short board work.

units.source: ### Chinese cleaver
units.masked_source: ### Chinese cleaver

⟦KBT0001⟧
  ⟦KBT0002⟧⟦KBT0003⟧⟦KBT0004⟧A Xinzuo Chinese-cleaver example; the exact specification determines whether it is a fine cutter or a heavier tool.⟦KBT0005⟧⟦KBT0006⟧
⟦KBT0007⟧

units.source: The Chinese cleaver is one of the most distinctive all-purpose forms. Its tall rectangular blade can slice, chop, guide against the knuckles, crush aromatics and transfer prepared ingredients. Examples vary greatly in weight and thickness, so the silhouette alone never proves that a knife can cut bone.

units.source: Its height, forward mass and lack of a familiar pointed profile can make it harder for beginners because they change the usual visual and tactile references for fine control. In experienced hands, the same features make it exceptionally versatile. Always check weight, thickness behind the edge, bevel geometry and intended use.
units.masked_source: Its height, forward mass and lack of a familiar pointed profile can make it harder for beginners because they change the usual visual and tactile references for fine control. In experienced hands, the same features make it exceptionally versatile. Always check weight, thickness behind the edge, bevel geometry and intended use.

units.source: On the board, a thin all-purpose Chinese cleaver works best with controlled push cuts, short vertical chops and draw slicing rather than heavy impact. The tall face gives excellent knuckle guidance and becomes a convenient scoop for moving prepared ingredients, but the broad blade also magnifies twisting forces if the edge becomes trapped in dense food. Treat a fine slicer as a slicer; use a true bone chopper only when its mass and edge geometry are designed for impact.

units.source: ### Bone chopper
units.masked_source: ### Bone chopper

⟦KBT0001⟧
  ⟦KBT0002⟧⟦KBT0003⟧⟦KBT0004⟧A Xinzuo bone-chopper example, built around mass and edge support rather than delicate slicing.⟦KBT0005⟧⟦KBT0006⟧
⟦KBT0007⟧

units.source: A bone chopper uses mass, a supported edge and substantial cross-section for controlled butchery where durability and momentum matter more than low-drag slicing. Steels and heat treatments for this work usually favour toughness over extreme hardness because the blade must absorb impact without failing suddenly.
units.masked_source: A bone chopper uses mass, a supported edge and substantial cross-section for controlled butchery where durability and momentum matter more than low-drag slicing. Steels and heat treatments for this work usually favour toughness over extreme hardness because the blade must absorb impact without failing suddenly.

units.source: It is not indestructible. Large dense bones, hard frozen material, unstable work or a glancing strike can damage the knife and injure the user. A thin Chinese cleaver may look similar while having completely different capabilities.
units.masked_source: It is not indestructible. Large dense bones, hard frozen material, unstable work or a glancing strike can damage the knife and injure the user. A thin Chinese cleaver may look similar while having completely different capabilities.

units.source: Technique should let the blade's mass do most of the work. Use a stable board, place the target securely and make a committed controlled stroke rather than repeated glancing blows. The thick supported edge is deliberately less delicate than a slicing edge, so using a bone chopper for fine vegetables or thin presentation slices trades accuracy and low drag for strength the task does not need.

units.source: ### Classic carving knife

⟦KBT0001⟧

⟦KBT0007⟧

units.source: A carving knife is longer and narrower than a chef's knife so it can cross a roast, poultry breast, boneless meat or large fruit with fewer strokes. Less blade height reduces drag and improves visibility. The intended movement is a long draw, not repeated short sawing.
units.masked_source: A carving knife is longer and narrower than a chef's knife so it can cross a roast, poultry breast, boneless meat or large fruit with fewer strokes. Less blade height reduces drag and improves visibility. The intended movement is a long draw, not repeated short sawing.

units.source: A useful carving stroke begins with as much of the edge as practical available in front of the food and pulls smoothly through the portion, using blade length instead of downward force. Compared with a chef's knife, the lower blade height gives less knuckle clearance on a board but offers better visibility around a roast and less side contact with the slice. Choose this form when long, clean portions matter more than chopping versatility.

units.source: ### Roast carving knife
units.masked_source: ### Roast carving knife

⟦KBT0001⟧
  ⟦KBT0002⟧⟦KBT0003⟧⟦KBT0004⟧A Xinzuo roast-carving example with a broader, upswept front.⟦KBT0005⟧⟦KBT0006⟧
⟦KBT0007⟧

units.source: The roast-carving profile keeps a long slicing edge but gives the front a pronounced upward curve. The curve follows the same geometric principle as the belly of a chef's knife: during a mainly horizontal draw, the changing angle of the curved edge creates a progressive downward component at the point of contact. This helps the edge penetrate the meat fibres as the blade moves across them instead of relying only on downward pressure. The curve also follows the rounded surface of a roast and lets the slice finish smoothly as the contact point moves toward the front. It remains a slicer for cooked, boneless food, not a joint breaker.

units.source: ### Ham knife
units.masked_source: ### Ham knife

⟦KBT0001⟧
  ⟦KBT0002⟧⟦KBT0003⟧⟦KBT0004⟧A Xinzuo ham-knife example, extra long and narrow for broad, thin slices.⟦KBT0005⟧⟦KBT0006⟧
⟦KBT0007⟧

units.source: A ham knife extends the carving-knife concept. Its very long, narrow blade produces broad thin slices with little friction. Some examples flex slightly to follow the ham; others are firmer. The design excels at long slicing but is inefficient for chopping and small board work.
units.masked_source: A ham knife extends the carving-knife concept. Its very long, narrow blade produces broad thin slices with little friction. Some examples flex slightly to follow the ham; others are firmer. The design excels at long slicing but is inefficient for chopping and small board work.

units.source: The extra length is valuable only when the cook uses it: start the cut near one end of the edge and let a long, light stroke travel through the meat. Mild flexibility can help the blade follow a broad curved surface, but it is not permission to bend or twist the knife sideways. Compared with a classic carving knife, the ham knife sacrifices some stiffness and general board control for exceptionally long, low-drag slicing.

units.source: Long traditional sashimi slicers use their length to cut raw fish in one pulling stroke, leaving a cleaner surface than repeated back-and-forth motion. Traditional examples are single bevelled, normally handed and sharpened differently from ordinary double-bevel slicers. This specialised geometry can steer if the user does not understand the bevel.
units.masked_source: Long traditional sashimi slicers use their length to cut raw fish in one pulling stroke, leaving a cleaner surface than repeated back-and-forth motion. Traditional examples are single bevelled, normally handed and sharpened differently from ordinary double-bevel slicers. This specialised geometry can steer if the user does not understand the bevel.

units.source: The technique is intentionally quiet: set the heel, draw the blade toward yourself in one continuous stroke and avoid sawing unless the cut genuinely requires a second pass. The long rigid profile and single-bevel geometry are optimized for surface quality and controlled separation, not for chopping or flexible filleting. Because the reverse face and main bevel form one sharpening system, this knife also demands more specialized maintenance than an ordinary double-bevel slicer.

units.source: The sakimaru belongs to the same long single-bevel slicing family but ends in a rounded, sword-influenced front. This changes balance, presentation and front access without changing the main task: clean draw slicing through boneless fish.

units.source: A Western boning knife is narrow because boning is a constantly changing three-dimensional cut. The edge must enter beside bone, follow joints, turn around curves, lift connective tissue and repeatedly change angle. A broad blade resists these changes once it is engaged in food. **The very small blade height is fundamental because it lets the blade change angle easily.**

The edge must enter beside bone, follow joints, turn around curves, lift connective tissue and repeatedly change angle. A broad blade resists these changes once it is engaged in food. **The very small blade height is fundamental because it lets the blade change angle easily.**

units.source: The narrow profile also improves visibility and control while tracing joints, removing connective tissue and separating meat from bone. Stiffer versions give deliberate control around beef and pork; more flexible versions follow rounded surfaces more easily.
units.masked_source: The narrow profile also improves visibility and control while tracing joints, removing connective tissue and separating meat from bone. Stiffer versions give deliberate control around beef and pork; more flexible versions follow rounded surfaces more easily.

units.source: Its main limitation is versatility. The narrow blade gives little knuckle clearance, little food-transfer area and less efficiency in broad board work than a chef's knife, gyuto or Chinese cleaver. Recommend it when boning is a recurring task, not as a general-purpose substitute. Boning means working **around** bone, not chopping through it; twisting the point or using it as a lever can still damage the knife.

units.source: ### Fillet knife
units.masked_source: ### Fillet knife

⟦KBT0001⟧
  ⟦KBT0002⟧⟦KBT0003⟧⟦KBT0004⟧A Xinzuo Western fillet-knife example, long and narrow enough to follow fish contours.⟦KBT0005⟧⟦KBT0006⟧
⟦KBT0007⟧

units.source: A Western fillet knife is long, narrow and often flexible. Its thin cross-section lets the blade follow a rib cage, stay close to skin and move around fish contours while leaving less flesh behind. It is a butchery tool that follows the fish's anatomy before presentation cuts, unlike a long rigid sashimi slicer designed mainly for a clean final draw cut.
units.masked_source: A Western fillet knife is long, narrow and often flexible. Its thin cross-section lets the blade follow a rib cage, stay close to skin and move around fish contours while leaving less flesh behind. It is a butchery tool that follows the fish's anatomy before presentation cuts, unlike a long rigid sashimi slicer designed mainly for a clean final draw cut.

units.source: Flexible models normally use a forgiving balance of toughness and hardness. **A fillet knife made from particularly hard steel needs more caution.** A hard thin blade can flex elastically, but it should never be forced into a deep bend, twisted against hard bone or used to test its flexibility. Excessive lateral stress can cause chipping, cracking or sudden fracture. A break can send the hand and broken edge in an uncontrolled direction, creating a real injury risk.

units.source: Use only the flex the model is designed to provide. If the knife feels forced rather than naturally following the contour, change the cutting angle instead of bending harder.

units.source: ### Deba

⟦KBT0001⟧

⟦KBT0007⟧

units.source: The deba is a thick, heavy fish-butchery knife. Its strong heel can work through appropriate fish joints and bones with controlled technique, while the front handles finer separation. Traditional deba are single bevelled and handed. Their weight does not make them universal cleavers: large mammal bone, twisting or careless impact can still chip the edge.
units.masked_source: The deba is a thick, heavy fish-butchery knife. units.source: The deba works by using different parts of the same blade for different operations. The thick heel provides support for controlled work through suitable fish joints and small fish bones, while the thinner front can trace around the head, collar and fillet line with much greater precision. Trying to make the tip perform the heel's impact work, or using the heel like a general-purpose meat cleaver, defeats that division of labour.

Its narrow profile reduces drag but gives less knuckle clearance and food-transfer area than a chef's knife.
units.masked_source: The utility knife is between a paring knife and a chef's knife in size and use. It has enough reach for fruit, sandwiches, small vegetables, cheese and boneless meat while remaining agile when a full-size blade would crowd the board. Its narrow profile reduces drag but gives less knuckle clearance and food-transfer area than a chef's knife.

units.source: It is especially useful in kitchens where many jobs are too large for a paring knife but do not justify the height and reach of a chef's knife: trimming a small roast, portioning citrus, cutting sandwiches or working on a crowded board. The compromise cuts both ways. It is more agile than a chef's knife but less efficient for large volumes, and more capable on a board than a paring knife but usually less comfortable for prolonged in-hand peeling.

units.source: ### Steak knife
units.masked_source: ### Steak knife

⟦KBT0001⟧

units.source: A steak knife cuts cooked meat at the table, and the choice between a **serrated** and a **plain** edge changes the eating experience.
units.masked_source: A steak knife cuts cooked meat at the table, and the choice between a **serrated** and a **plain** edge changes the eating experience.

units.source: A serrated steak knife can remain **apparently sharp for a long time**. The serration points continue to grip the meat even after repeated plate contact, and the teeth can cut and tear fibres after a smooth edge would feel dull. This makes the knife forgiving in everyday service. The trade-off is a rougher cut: serrations partly tear the meat, disturb its texture and can rupture more cells at the surface, allowing more juice to escape. This may be acceptable for inexpensive or casual service but is less suitable for high-quality meat.

units.source: For premium steak, a **very sharp plain-edge steak knife** gives a cleaner cut and preserves texture and appearance better. Its weakness is the plate. When every stroke ends against ceramic, the fine apex repeatedly strikes a much harder surface and can lose sharpness quickly.

units.source: For valuable meat, the best arrangement is simple: **use a sharp plain-edge steak knife and complete the cut on a wooden plate or small food-safe wooden board rather than directly on ceramic**. If ceramic tableware is unavoidable, the edge will need more frequent maintenance.

units.source: ### Cheese knife
units.masked_source: ### Cheese knife

⟦KBT0001⟧
  ⟦KBT0002⟧⟦KBT0003⟧⟦KBT0004⟧A Xinzuo cheese-knife example; different cheese textures still call for different handling.⟦KBT0005⟧⟦KBT0006⟧

units.source: Cheese knives are a family, not one universal shape. Soft sticky cheese benefits from less contact area; a narrow point can portion and serve; hard aged cheese needs stronger support. Openings, hollows and other relief can reduce sticking but cannot eliminate it for every cheese. Choose according to the cheese's texture and size, not the category name alone.

Soft sticky cheese benefits from less contact area; a narrow point can portion and serve; hard aged cheese needs stronger support. Openings, hollows and other relief can reduce sticking but cannot eliminate it for every cheese. Choose according to the cheese's texture and size, not the category name alone.

units.source: Think first about the mechanical problem: soft cheese tends to adhere to broad faces, crumbly cheese rewards a controlled wedge, and very hard cheese needs enough spine and edge support to resist twisting. A cheese knife is therefore best treated as a texture-specific tool rather than a decorative serving pattern. When the cheese is large or dense, stabilize it before cutting; forcing a thin point sideways can damage both knife and food.

units.source: ### Bread knife

⟦KBT0001⟧
  ⟦KBT0002⟧⟦KBT0003⟧⟦KBT0004⟧A Xinzuo bread-knife example with a long serrated edge.⟦KBT0005⟧⟦KBT0006⟧

units.source: Bread-knife serrations solve a simple problem: entering a resistant surface and cutting a soft interior **without compressing it first**. Historically, breadmaking, storage and common loaf styles made this especially useful, but the principle still applies today.
units.masked_source: Bread-knife serrations solve a simple problem: entering a resistant surface and cutting a soft interior **without compressing it first**. Historically, breadmaking, storage and common loaf styles made this especially useful, but the principle still applies today.

units.source: The teeth grip the surface so the user can make a light drawing or sawing motion instead of pressing hard downward. Several small contact points let the blade advance with less crushing of the crumb or other soft structure.
units.masked_source: The teeth grip the surface so the user can make a light drawing or sawing motion instead of pressing hard downward. Several small contact points let the blade advance with less crushing of the crumb or other soft structure.

units.source: A pronounced saw profile is **not always necessary** for modern bread. Crust, crumb and freshness vary, and a very sharp plain edge can cut many loaves cleanly. Serrations are most useful when the surface resists first contact but the interior deforms easily. They also work extremely well on brioche, panettone, soft rolls and cake, where downward pressure can deform the product before a plain edge starts the cut.

units.source: Use a light guided sawing motion and let the teeth work. Excessive pressure crushes the crumb. Serrations often stay functional for a long time because their recesses receive less direct board contact, but sharpening is less straightforward and may require a tapered sharpener or specialist service.

units.source: ### Frozen-food knife
units.masked_source: ### Frozen-food knife

⟦KBT0001⟧
  ⟦KBT0002⟧⟦KBT0003⟧⟦KBT0004⟧A Xinzuo frozen-food-knife example with a coarse scalloped edge.⟦KBT0005⟧⟦KBT0006⟧

units.source: A frozen-food knife uses strong coarse serrations to saw through suitable frozen ingredients. It exists because forcing a thin hard chef's knife into a frozen block can chip or break the blade. This is still a hazardous specialist operation: stabilize the food, keep the free hand outside the cutting path and avoid twisting or impact.

units.source: Use the full serrated length with short, controlled strokes and keep the blade aligned with the cut. Do not pry the kerf open or twist the knife when it binds; reposition the food and restart. The specialist geometry reduces the temptation to strike a frozen block with a fine chef's knife, but it does not make every frozen item safe or practical to cut by hand.

units.source: ## Choosing by work rather than by name
units.masked_source: ## Choosing by work rather than by name

units.source: For most kitchens, the first serious knife should be a chef's knife, gyuto, santoku or Chinese cleaver whose length and movement feel natural. A bread knife and a small utility or paring knife then cover jobs the main blade handles poorly. Long carving, filleting, fish-butchery and impact tools become worthwhile when those tasks occur often enough to justify dedicated geometry.

units.source: For sales staff, return to the same questions: **What foods will the customer cut most often? In what quantities? On a board or in the hand? Does the work need broad contact, a long draw, controlled flexibility, a precise point, constant angle changes around bone, or supported mass for impact?** Once the work is clear, the right family of shapes is usually clear too.
